Reviewer #1:

This manuscript presents previously undescribed features of nuclear envelope breakdown at the onset of meiosis in starfish oocytes. Using these same cells the authors previously uncovered a role for actin filaments in confining chromosomes and facilitating their capture by spindle microtubules. They also demonstrated that nuclear envelope breakdown in starfish oocytes requires transient assembly of a branched actin network on the inner surface of the nuclear envelope (Mori et al., 2014). The 2014 Current Biology paper reported the presence of radially oriented actin bundles, or spikes, growing out of a lamin-associated actin network and into the nuclear envelope. At the time the authors interpreted the role of these spikes as puncturing or forcefully fragmenting the nuclear envelope.

In the current work the authors have employed higher resolution light microscopy techniques to characterize the spatial relationships between the actin filaments, the nuclear envelope, the nuclear lamins, and the nuclear pore complexes. The major result is that the role of actin assembly appears to be 'delamination' of the nucleus by prying the nuclear envelope away from the underlying nuclear lamins. This is not a brand new mechanism but certainly represents a refinement of the previous view of actin's role in NEB in this system. I am inclined to think it justifies publication as a brief report, but there are a few points that should be addressed before publication.

1) The authors previously localized the Arp2/3 complex to the nuclear actin shell (in the 2014 Curr Biol paper), but they show no Arp2/3 localization in the current paper. They should use their super-resolution light microscopy to investigate the relationship between Arp2/3, filamentous actin, and the nuclear envelope. My suspicion is that the Arp2/3 will be associated with the lamins, but not with the actin spikes or the overlying nuclear envelope.

2) Which nucleation promoting factors are activating the Arp2/3 complex in this system? The obvious candidate is WASP. Do any WASP antibodies cross-react with the starfish protein?

3) The filopodia-like morphology of the actin spikes suggests that perhaps some nuclear envelope-associated polymerase is promoting filament elongation. Have the authors looked for VASP et al. on the inner surface of the nuclear envelope?

Reviewer #2:

In this manuscript, Wesolowska et al. use super-resolution light and electron microscopy in combination to study how actin contributes to nuclear envelope rupture in starfish oocytes. This builds upon previous work from the team published in Current Biology that described an important role for Arp2.3 nucleated actin spikes in NEB.

In their new paper, the authors study the ultrastructure in more detail. They show that nuclear envelope is uniform and densely packed with NPCs in immature oocytes, before becoming heterogeneous with the generation of actin spikes, when it breaks up into regions that have a high or low density of NPCs prior to nuclear envelope rupture. The authors argue that the actin filaments nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex embedded within the nuclear lamina push on the nuclear envelope to induce membrane deformations (bumps and spikes), which lead to the separation of NPCs-free and NPCs-rich membranes and to subsequent ruptures of the envelope.

The paper is well written, and the data are presented clearly. There is some valuable new information about how the ultrastructure of the nuclear envelope evolves from immature oocyte to the NEBD with a complete rupture of the nuclear envelope. Some questions remain, however, about precisely how actin spikes contributes to rupture.

In the model depicted in Figure 6, the key events are 1) A mitotic specific change in NPCs 2) The actin-dependent partitioning of NPCs into rich and poor regions. 3) Rupture.

This series of events is not exactly demonstrated in the data:

1) In several figures, such as Figure 4C, there are gaps in the organization of NPCs without deformation of the inner nuclear membrane (bumps neither spikes). The authors mention as well that "gaps appeared to evolve into bumps and membrane spikes". Doesn't this suggest that NPCs-free membrane areas are generated prior to actin spikes rather than "by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free, ER-like membrane networks".

2) The paper doesn't do enough to explain how changes in NPCs themselves contribute to this process. Where does NPC re-modelling come into the picture?

3) The link between membrane rupture and local actin spikes remains a bit unclear. In images, the most obvious effect of an actin spike is the separation of inner and outer envelopes. One might then expect rupture within spike regions to sometimes break one membrane – which would seem a very bad thing to do. Isn't it more likely that in the end rupture occurs via NPC disassembly as in other systems – but that this is membrane tension (and therefore actin) dependent ?

Reviewer #3:

Nuclear envelope breakdown is a fundamental feature of the cell cycle in most animal cells and yet its basis remains poorly understood. In the textbook view, it somehow arises as a consequence of phosphorylation of lamins and components of the nuclear envelope such as the nucleoporins. There is also evidence that cell cycle-regulated, microtubule motor-dependent transport can tear the envelope in some cell types and that polymerizing actin can tear it in other cell types. But in neither case, has the process been studied in anywhere near sufficient detail for anything more than vague conclusions to be drawn.

In the current study, using a careful combination of light and electron microscopy, the authors have obtained evidence that during the disassembly of the germinal vesicle (the large oocyte nucleus) in starfish, spikes of actin that assemble from within the nuclear lamina drive evagination of the nuclear envelope concomitant with displacement of the nuclear pore complexes. That is, as the spikes extend outward (i.e. toward the cytoplasm) the nuclear pore complexes are left behind in patches flanking the spikes while the nuclear envelope overlying the spikes is nuclear pore complex-free. The authors propose that the evaginations of pore-free envelope are unstable and consequently rupture.

This is fascinating, and beautifully executed work. However, the authors should address the following points before their conclusions can be accepted with confidence.

1) The authors need to marshal quantitative support for their main conclusions. As far as I can tell, there is just a single image in the paper that shows actin filaments inside one of the evaginations (Figure 4E). Thus, it is important to know just how frequent this phenomenon is. This point is particularly important given the fact that the authors have shown that when F-actin assembly is suppressed by CK666, the nuclear envelope nonetheless becomes uneven. Other points that would benefit from quantification include the relative density of nuclear pores in evaginations versus the shoulders of evaginations.

2) The authors state "Our EM data clearly show that the F-actin shell protrudes pore-free nuclear membranes, separating these from the lamina". This is not quite true as there are no EM data showing the envelope under conditions where the shell is prevented from forming. Such data should be provided. The fluorescence imaging does not allow this point to be tested as the membrane cannot be seen.

3) The authors also conclude that the pore-free membrane is unstable and thus serves as the site of ruptures. However, unless I missed it, there is no evidence that the ruptures arise first at the points of the evaginations. Given that one of the goals of the study is to understand how rupturing occurs, the authors need to address this point by determining whether the rupture occurs at the tips of spikes, at the shoulders of spikes, or elsewhere.

claims.claim: Breakdown of the specialized nuclear envelope in starfish oocytes is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin 'shell', in contrast to microtubule-driven tearing in mammalian fibroblasts.
claims.source: We showed that breakdown of this specialized NE is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin 'shell' in starfish oocytes, in contrast to microtubule-driven tearing in mammalian fibroblasts.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014) and contrasts with established mechanisms in mammalian cells (Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002).

claims.claim: Actin is nucleated within the lamina, sprouting filopodia-like spikes towards the nuclear membranes.
claims.source: We show that actin is nucleated within the lamina, sprouting filopodia-like spikes towards the nuclear membranes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data showing F-actin spikes extending from the lamina (Figure 3D, E) and EM data showing membrane protrusions with fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments (Figure 5D, E).

claims.claim: F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes, whereas the adjoining stretches of membrane accumulate NPCs that are associated with the still-intact lamina.
claims.source: These F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes, whereas the adjoining stretches of membrane accumulate NPCs that are associated with the still-intact lamina.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by EM showing membrane spikes free of NPCs with NPC-dense regions at their base (Figure 5D, G), and STED imaging showing similar patterns (Figure 5G).

claims.claim: Packed NPCs sort into a distinct membrane network, while breaks appear in ER-like, pore-free regions.
claims.source: Packed NPCs sort into a distinct membrane network, while breaks appear in ER-like, pore-free regions.
claims.evidence: This is supported by EM data showing NPC-dense nucleoplasmic bodies and rupture occurring in pore-free membrane regions (Figures 6, 7A).

claims.claim: The nuclear envelope is composed of inner and outer nuclear membranes that are fused at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) to mediate nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
claims.source: The nuclear envelope (NE), composed of inner and outer nuclear membranes, is a specialized sub-compartment of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that separates the nucleus and the cytoplasm in eukaryotic cells. The inner and outer NE is fused at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) to mediate nucleo-cytoplasmic transport.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about nuclear envelope structure, supported by citation to Burke and Ellenberg, 2002.

claims.claim: The lamina is a network of intermediate filaments that lines the nucleoplasmic side of the nuclear envelope and provides mechanical support.
claims.source: This complex NE membrane structure is mechanically supported by a network of intermediate filaments, the lamina, which lines the nucleoplasmic side (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about lamina structure and function, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Oocytes have an exceptionally large nucleus known as the germinal vesicle.
claims.source: Oocytes have a very specialized nuclear architecture with an exceptionally large nucleus, also known as the germinal vesicle, which stores nuclear components that are necessary to support early embryonic development.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about oocyte nuclear structure.

claims.claim: The oocyte nuclear envelope is densely packed with NPCs that serve as a stockpile for early embryonic development.
claims.source: The oocyte NE is densely packed with NPCs that serve as a stockpile of these complexes (rendering oocytes a popular model in which to study NPCs), and the lamina is thick so that it is able to provide mechanical support for this very large structure (Goldberg and Allen, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldberg and Allen, 1995, and is consistent with the EM data showing high NPC density (Figure 5A, B).

claims.claim: In vertebrates and deuterostomes (including the echinoderm starfish), the complex NE structure is fully disassembled during division.
claims.source: In Drosophila and Caenorhabditis elegans embryos, the NE and the lamina remains partially intact during cell division, whereas in vertebrates and deuterostomes (including the echinoderm starfish), the complex NE structure is fully disassembled during division.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in NE disassembly across species.

claims.claim: In somatic mammalian cells, NE disassembly involves the complete dismantling of the NPCs, depolymerization of the lamina, and re-absorption of the nuclear membranes into the ER.
claims.source: In somatic mammalian cells, NE disassembly involves the complete dismantling of the NPCs, depolymerization of the lamina, and re-absorption of the nuclear membranes into the ER (Hetzer, 2010; Ungricht and Kutay, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hetzer, 2010 and Ungricht and Kutay, 2017.

claims.claim: NEBD begins with a partial permeabilization of the NE resulting from phosphorylation-driven disassembly of the NPCs and other NE components.
claims.source: In all species in which nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) has been investigated in detail, including somatic cells and oocytes from various species, NEBD begins with a partial permeabilization of the NE resulting from phosphorylation-driven disassembly of the NPCs and other NE components (Dultz et al., 2008; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007; Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003; Martino et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations documenting this mechanism across species.

claims.claim: During the first phase of NEBD, partial permeabilization allows proteins and smaller dextrans up to ~70 kDa to leak in or out of the nucleus.
claims.source: This allows proteins, and smaller dextrans up to ~70 kDa, to leak in or out of the nucleus (Lénárt et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Lénárt et al., 2003, and is consistent with the experimental use of 25 kDa dextran as a marker of partial permeabilization (Figure 4A, B).

claims.claim: During the first phase of NEBD, the overall structure of the NE is still intact and the compartmentalization of large protein complexes is maintained.
claims.source: Importantly, however, during this first phase of NEBD, the overall structure of the NE (as observed by electron microscopy (EM)) is still intact and the compartmentalization of large protein complexes (e.g. ribosomes and microtubules) is maintained (Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Terasaki et al., 2001 and Lénárt et al., 2003.

claims.claim: In cultured mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process.
claims.source: In cultured mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process (Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Beaudouin et al., 2002 and Salina et al., 2002.

claims.claim: In the large oocyte nucleus, the actin cytoskeleton rather than the microtubule cytoskeleton is required for NE rupture.
claims.source: By contrast, we have shown recently that in the large oocyte nucleus, the actin cytoskeleton rather than the microtubule cytoskeleton is required for NE rupture.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014) and the current data showing F-actin shell formation and its requirement for NE rupture (Figures 1, 2).

claims.claim: A transient F-actin 'shell' is polymerized by the Arp2/3 complex on the inner surface of the NE and membranes undergo complete rupture within two minutes of its formation.
claims.source: A transient F-actin 'shell' is polymerized by the Arp2/3 complex on the inner surface of the NE and membranes undergo complete rupture within two minutes of its formation (Mori et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Mori et al., 2014 and the current live-cell imaging data (Figure 1A).

claims.claim: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans.
claims.source: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans (Figure 1A, 0 s).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Approximately 30–45 s after the F-actin shell first appears, as the F-actin foci grow and intensify, merging to form a continuous F-actin shell, the first breaks on the NE appear, allowing a large 500 kDa dextran to flood into the nucleus.
claims.source: Approximately 30–45 s later, as the F-actin foci grow and intensify, merging to form a continuous F-actin shell, the first breaks on the NE appear, allowing a large 500 kDa dextran to flood into the nucleus (Figure 1A, 45 s).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The F-actin shell spreads towards the poles before a wave of membrane rupture takes place after a delay of ~30 s.
claims.source: The shell then spreads towards the poles before a wave of membrane rupture takes place after a delay of ~30 s (Figure 1A, 90 s).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: As the first F-actin foci began to assemble, the NE still appeared smooth and continuous.
claims.source: When we looked at the process with our new approach, we saw that as the first F-actin foci began to assemble, the NE still appeared smooth and continuous, as visualized by a membrane probe (DiIC18(3)) and a marker of NPCs (a fragment of importin-β) (Figure 1B, −13 s).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in high-resolution live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: 10–15 s after F-actin foci begin to assemble, the first spike-like membrane protrusions towards the cytoplasm are observed, which then rapidly escalate into a complex, convoluted and fragmented membrane structure.
claims.source: 10–15 s later, we observed the first spike-like membrane protrusions towards the cytoplasm, which then rapidly escalated into a complex, convoluted and fragmented membrane structure (Figure 1B–D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in high-resolution live-cell imaging data shown in Figures 1B-D.

claims.claim: During membrane reorganization, NPCs appeared to separate partially from the membrane towards the nucleoplasmic side.
claims.source: Intriguingly, during this process NPCs appeared to separate partially from the membrane towards the nucleoplasmic side.
claims.evidence: This is observed in live-cell imaging data (Figure 1B) and confirmed by STED microscopy (Figure 3C).

claims.claim: Dextran entry did not coincide with the formation of the initial membrane spikes, it occurred 20–30 s later, when membrane reorganization had progressed to a rather advanced stage.
claims.source: Dextran entry did not coincide with the formation of the initial membrane spikes, it occurred 20–30 s later, when membrane reorganization had progressed to a rather advanced stage (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Membrane reorganization is dependent on actin assembly.
claims.source: This membrane reorganization is dependent on actin assembly.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments showing that inhibiting F-actin shell formation by depleting actin monomers prevents membrane reorganization (Figure 1E).

claims.claim: If the F-actin shell is inhibited by injecting a large amount of the actin-binding UtrCH domain to deplete available actin monomers, the NE membrane stays smooth and continuous.
claims.source: If the F-actin shell is inhibited by injecting a large amount of the actin-binding UtrCH domain to deplete available actin monomers, the NE membrane stays smooth and continuous (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: Even when F-actin shell formation is inhibited, the nucleus does collapse and the NE ruffles and folds as a result of the progressing partial NE disassembly.
claims.source: Even in this case, the nucleus does collapse and the NE ruffles and folds as a result of the progressing partial NE disassembly.
claims.evidence: This is observed in experiments with UtrCH-mediated actin depletion (Figure 1E) and is consistent with previous work (Mori et al., 2014).

claims.claim: When F-actin shell formation is inhibited, large and folded membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD.
claims.source: However, unlike in control oocytes, these large and folded membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD, as we showed in earlier work (Mori et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Mori et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In starfish oocytes, actin assembly mediates a reorganization of nuclear membranes that leads to NE rupture.
claims.source: Thus, we concluded that, in starfish oocytes, actin assembly mediates a reorganization of nuclear membranes that leads to NE rupture.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the live-cell imaging data showing membrane reorganization dependent on F-actin assembly (Figures 1B-E).

claims.claim: The endogenous lamin network remains continuous even minutes after NE rupture, although it folds and ruffles as the nucleus collapses during NEBD.
claims.source: This confirmed our previous observations that the endogenous lamin network remains continuous even minutes after NE rupture, although it folds and ruffles as the nucleus collapses during NEBD (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B and is consistent with previous observations.

claims.claim: The lamin mesh gradually coarsens during the process of NEBD.
claims.source: In addition, imaging portions of the lamina en face by stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy suggests that the lamin mesh gradually coarsens during the process of NEBD (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The rupture of the NE does not proceed by F-actin-induced tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina, which remains a continuous network throughout NEBD.
claims.source: We conclude that the rupture of the NE does not proceed by F-actin-induced tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina, which remains a continuous network throughout NEBD.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on immunofluorescence and STED data showing continuous lamina throughout NEBD (Figure 2B).

claims.claim: The lamina co-localized with phalloidin, while the NPC staining formed a separate layer of fragmented appearance up to 500 nm 'above' the F-actin shell.
claims.source: We observed that although the lamina co-localized with phalloidin, the NPC staining formed a separate layer of fragmented appearance up to 500 nm 'above' the F-actin shell (Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in immunofluorescence data with line profile analysis shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: The still-intact lamina appears to serve as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, whereas the nuclear membranes appear to fragment and separate away from the lamina and the F-actin shell.
claims.source: Thus, the still-intact lamina appears to serve as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, whereas the nuclear membranes appear to fragment and separate away from the lamina and the F-actin shell.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data showing lamina with F-actin and separation of NPCs/membranes (Figures 3A, B).

claims.claim: Before NE rupture, the NPC and lamina stainings overlapped at the approx. 50 nm resolution afforded by STED, which is consistent with the known ultrastructure of the NE.
claims.source: Before NE rupture, the NPC and lamina stainings overlapped at the approx. 50 nm resolution afforded by STED, which is consistent with the known ultrastructure of the NE (Figure 3C, pre-NEBD) (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in STED data (Figure 3C) and is consistent with established knowledge (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002).

claims.claim: At the shell stage, NPC-stained NE fragments 'float' above the intact lamina.
claims.source: In stark contrast, at the shell stage, we were able to visualize NPC-stained NE fragments 'floating' above the intact lamina (Figure 3C, post-NEBD).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in STED data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The separation of lamina and membranes is dependent on the F-actin shell.
claims.source: This separation of lamina and membranes is dependent on the F-actin shell, because this process did not occur when we prevented F-actin shell formation by inhibiting Arp2/3 using the small molecule inhibitor CK-666 (Figure 3C, post-NEBD + CK-666).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data using CK-666 inhibitor shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: STED imaging of optimally fixed samples revealed filopodia-like F-actin spikes of 0.5–2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm, and extending from the base of the F-actin shell towards the nuclear membranes.
claims.source: STED imaging of samples that were optimally fixed for phalloidin staining revealed filopodia-like F-actin spikes of 0.5–2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm, and extending from the base of the F-actin shell towards the nuclear membranes (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed and measured in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The Arp2/3 complex is localized at the base of the F-actin shell just beneath the NE, whereas the F-actin spikes extending from the base are not labeled by ArpC1.
claims.source: Furthermore, using a starfish-specific anti-ArpC1 antibody, we localized the Arp2/3 complex at the base of the F-actin shell just beneath the NE, whereas the F-actin spikes extending from the base were not labeled by ArpC1 (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data with ArpC1 antibody staining shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs, most probably because NPCs are still attached to the lamina, and thus NPCs are held back and cluster at the base of spikes.
claims.source: Membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs, most probably because NPCs are still attached to the lamina, and thus NPCs are held back and cluster at the base of spikes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from EM and STED data showing pore-free spikes with NPC clusters at their base (Figures 5D, G).

claims.claim: The NE is smooth, continuous and is tightly packed with NPCs with a regular spacing of ~200 nm in immature oocytes, as well as in oocytes just before NE rupture and even in the intact polar regions of the NE undergoing rupture.
claims.source: First, as consistent with earlier observations, the NE is smooth, continuous and is tightly packed with NPCs with a regular spacing of ~200 nm in immature oocytes, as well as in oocytes just before NE rupture and even in the intact polar regions of the NE undergoing rupture (see Figure 5A,B for image examples, and Figure 6C for quantification) (Lénárt et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figures 5A, B) with quantification (Figure 6C) and is consistent with previous observations (Lénárt et al., 2003).

claims.claim: In areas closer to the rupture site, regions with gaps in NPC occupancy are observed, the number and size of which increased proximal to this region.
claims.source: By contrast, in areas closer to the rupture site, we observed regions with gaps in NPC occupancy, the number and size of which increased proximal to this region (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: In the vicinity of the rupture site, gaps appeared to evolve into 'bumps' and membrane spikes.
claims.source: In the vicinity of the site, gaps appeared to evolve into 'bumps' and membrane spikes (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The most prominent spikes observed rose ~1 µm above the level of the NE.
claims.source: Although reconstructing the full 3D architecture of these spikes is challenging, even in 300-nm-thick tomographic sections, the most prominent spikes that we observed rose ~1 µm above the level of the NE (Figure 5D,E).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured in EM and tomographic data shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claims.claim: Membrane spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments.
claims.source: These spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) and are even more clearly distinguishable on tomographic reconstructions (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM and tomographic data shown in Figure 5D, E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Membrane spikes observed by EM were covered by continuous nuclear membranes and almost completely free of NPCs.
claims.source: Intriguingly, on both thin sections and tomographic reconstructions, we observed that these spikes were covered by continuous nuclear membranes and almost completely free of NPCs (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM and tomographic data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Pore-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell are surrounded by NPC-dense adjacent regions.
claims.source: These pore-free areas are surrounded by NPC-dense adjacent regions (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause the crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions.
claims.source: We are unable to estimate the 3D membrane areas from 2D sections, nevertheless, our data suggest that NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause the crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from EM observations and quantification of NPC spacing shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: The lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters.
claims.source: In addition, we were able to visualize that the lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters, suggesting that NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina.
claims.source: In addition, we were able to visualize that the lamina runs at the base of the F-actin shell, below but still attached to NPC clusters, suggesting that NPCs might be held back at the base of spikes by their attachments to the lamina (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from STED microscopy data showing lamina at the base of F-actin shell with attached NPC clusters (Figure 5G).

claims.claim: The growing gaps between NPCs develop into bumps and spikes that are protrusions generated by Arp2/3-driven actin polymerization, which pries nuclear membranes and lamina apart.
claims.source: Together, our data from EM correlated with live cell and immunofluorescence suggest that the growing gaps between NPCs, which then develop into bumps and spikes, are protrusions generated by Arp2/3-driven actin polymerization, which pries nuclear membranes and lamina apart.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including EM, live-cell imaging, and immunofluorescence (Figures 3, 5).

claims.claim: In regions closer to rupture sites, an increasing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments is observed.
claims.source: In regions closer to rupture sites, we observed an increasing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies are dense, round structures 200–500 nm in diameter beneath the NE in the nucleoplasm.
claims.source: Furthermore, accompanying spikes and NPC-rich clusters, we observed additional frequent membrane structures, which we call nucleoplasmic bodies. These are dense, round structures 200–500 nm in diameter beneath the NE in the nucleoplasm (Figures 5D and 6B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed and measured in EM data shown in Figures 5D and 6B.

claims.claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement with a slightly electron-denser material connecting them.
claims.source: These bodies often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement with a slightly electron-denser material connecting them (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Above nucleoplasmic bodies, the NE appears to be still intact, consisting mostly of NPC-free nuclear membranes and maintaining the nucleo-cytoplasmic boundary, as judged by the distribution of ribosomes.
claims.source: Above them, the NE appears to be still intact, consisting mostly of NPC-free nuclear membranes and maintaining the nucleo-cytoplasmic boundary, as judged by the distribution of ribosomes.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figure 6B) based on ribosome distribution.

claims.claim: In pore-dense segments and nucleoplasmic bodies, pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm.
claims.source: In pore-dense segments, as well as in nucleoplasmic bodies, our quantification shows that pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm (Figure 6C), suggesting that the NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured and quantified from EM data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
claims.source: In pore-dense segments, as well as in nucleoplasmic bodies, our quantification shows that pore-to-pore distance decreased substantially from ~200 nm in intact areas to ~100 nm (Figure 6C), suggesting that the NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the quantification of NPC spacing showing increased density in some regions and decreased density in others (Figure 6C).

claims.claim: Nucleoplasmic bodies may form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters, initially inducing pits that curve into the nucleoplasm and then forming inverted NE tubules filled inside with cytoplasm.
claims.source: Careful examination of intermediates suggests that nucleoplasmic bodies may form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters, initially inducing pits that curve into the nucleoplasm and then forming inverted NE tubules filled inside with cytoplasm (Figure 6A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from examination of EM intermediates shown in Figures 6A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The electron density along the boundary of nucleoplasmic bodies corresponds to closely juxtaposed NPCs with an intact central ring structure, similar to NPCs in still-intact areas.
claims.source: Sections capturing these structures en face and tomograms confirm that the electron density along the boundary of the bodies corresponds to closely juxtaposed NPCs with an intact central ring structure, similar to NPCs in still-intact areas (see 'nucleoplasmic bodies' in Figure 6D,E).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM sections and tomograms shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claims.claim: The membranes were interrupted in areas where the segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions was strongest and NPC invaginations frequent and most dramatic.
claims.source: Finally, the EM montages revealed that the membranes were interrupted in areas where the segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions was strongest and NPC invaginations frequent and most dramatic (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM montages shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: In areas of membrane rupture, no continuous membrane boundary was seen to separate cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies were abundant.
claims.source: Here, no continuous membrane boundary was seen to separate cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies were abundant.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in EM data (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Light microscopy of the stage corresponding to membrane rupture revealed a complex tubular-vesicular network that was densely labeled by NPC staining.
claims.source: Light microscopy of the corresponding stage revealed a complex tubular-vesicular network that was densely labeled by NPC staining, occasionally resolving cross-sections of tubules consistent with our EM data (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in STED microscopy data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments.
claims.source: Together, our data show that NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence from EM, live-cell imaging, and immunofluorescence showing membrane segregation (Figures 5, 6, 7).

claims.claim: Pore-dense segments invaginate, forming a network of nucleoplasmic bodies, whereas rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments.
claims.source: Pore-dense segments invaginate, forming a network of nucleoplasmic bodies, whereas rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on EM data showing invaginating NPC-dense regions and rupture in pore-free regions (Figures 6, 7).

claims.claim: F-actin foci form within the lamina when cytoplasmic components, such as the Arp2/3 complex and actin monomers, reach a critical concentration in the nucleus as a result of the gradual, phosphorylation-driven disassembly and increasing leakiness of the NPCs in the first phase of NEBD.
claims.source: We hypothesize that these foci form at the time when cytoplasmic components, such as the Arp2/3 complex and actin monomers, reach a critical concentration in the nucleus as a result of the gradual, phosphorylation-driven disassembly and increasing leakiness of the NPCs in the first phase of NEBD.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known mechanism of NPC disassembly and the observed timing of F-actin foci formation.

claims.claim: Once triggered, F-actin foci grow rapidly, which is expected as a result of the autocatalytic nature of Arp2/3-mediated nucleation of branched F-actin networks.
claims.source: Once triggered, F-actin foci grow rapidly, which is expected as a result of the autocatalytic nature of Arp2/3-mediated nucleation of branched F-actin networks.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Arp2/3-mediated actin polymerization and is consistent with the observed rapid growth of F-actin foci (Figure 1A).

claims.claim: The filaments seem to grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes, and push against them.
claims.source: As the foci spread, they merge to form a continuous shell. The filaments seem to grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes, and push against them.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observed morphology of F-actin spikes extending from the lamina towards membranes (Figures 3D, 5D, E).

claims.claim: The asymmetry in filament growth may be explained by the fact that force imposed on actin filaments promotes the nucleation of a branched meshwork.
claims.source: This asymmetry may be explained by the fact that force imposed on actin filaments promotes the nucleation of a branched meshwork (Bieling et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on established knowledge from Bieling et al., 2016.

claims.claim: F-actin networks that are nucleated in vitro on micropatterned activated Arp2/3 show a morphology that is strikingly similar to that of the F-actin shell, with filopodia-like bundles pointing away from a base of dense branched network.
claims.source: Intriguingly, F-actin networks that are nucleated in vitro on micropatterned activated Arp2/3 show a morphology that is strikingly similar to that of the F-actin shell, with filopodia-like bundles pointing away from a base of dense branched network (Reymann et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Reymann et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Localized activation of Arp2/3 within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the morphology of the F-actin shell.
claims.source: This suggests that localized activation of Arp2/3 within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the morphology of the F-actin shell.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the similarity to in vitro F-actin networks (Reymann et al., 2010) and the observed localization of Arp2/3 at the base of the shell (Figure 3E).

claims.claim: The F-actin shell protrudes pore-free nuclear membranes, separating these from the lamina, because most NPCs are attached to the still-intact lamina at this stage, and thus are held back, while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.
claims.source: Our light and electron microscopy data clearly show that the F-actin shell protrudes pore-free nuclear membranes, separating these from the lamina. We propose that these membranes are cleared of NPCs, because most NPCs are attached to the still-intact lamina at this stage, and thus are held back, while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.

results.result: Nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD) in starfish oocytes is mediated by an Arp2/3-nucleated F-actin shell, which destabilizes the NE by segregating pore-dense and pore-free membranes. This mechanism contrasts with microtubule-driven tearing observed in mammalian somatic cells and provides the first mechanistic explanation for the sudden collapse of the NE structure during its breakdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C15, C16, and C88 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including live-cell imaging (Figure 1A), EM data (Figures 5-7), STED microscopy (Figures 3, 5G), and inhibitor experiments (Figures 1E, 3C). The data consistently demonstrate that F-actin assembly is required for NE rupture and that this mechanism differs from the microtubule-driven process in mammalian cells. The conclusion is based on comprehensive structural and functional data.

results.result: Actin is nucleated by the Arp2/3 complex within the lamina and forms filopodia-like spikes (0.5-2 μm in length, spaced at ~0.1 μm) that extend towards and protrude nuclear membranes. These spikes contain fibrous densities consistent with actin filaments and grow preferentially from the shell base in the lamina towards nuclear membranes.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C37, C38, C45, C51, and C67 are strongly supported by STED microscopy showing F-actin spikes with precise measurements (Figure 3D), EM and tomographic data showing membrane protrusions with actin filaments (Figures 5D, E), and ArpC1 localization at the base of the shell (Figure 3E). The morphology and dimensions are consistently observed across multiple imaging modalities.

results.result: F-actin spikes protrude pore-free nuclear membranes while NPCs accumulate at the base of spikes, remaining attached to the still-intact lamina. The membrane evaginations are largely free of NPCs because NPCs are held back by their attachments to the lamina while membranes are protruded by actin assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C40, C46, C47, C49, C50, and C71 are well-supported by EM data showing membrane spikes free of NPCs with NPC-dense regions at their base (Figures 5D, G), STED imaging showing similar patterns (Figure 5G), and quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C). The proposed mechanism that NPCs are held back by lamina attachments is a reasonable inference from the structural data.

results.result: The lamina remains continuous throughout NEBD, gradually coarsening but not undergoing rapid disassembly or F-actin-induced tearing. The NE rupture does not proceed by tearing or rapid disassembly of the lamina.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C30, and C31 are supported by immunofluorescence data showing continuous lamina throughout NEBD (Figure 2B) and STED microscopy showing gradual coarsening of the lamin mesh (Figure 2B). This conclusion is consistent with previous observations and contrasts with the microtubule-driven tearing mechanism in somatic cells.

results.result: NE rupture proceeds by F-actin-driven sorting of NE membranes into pore-dense and pore-free segments. Pore-dense segments invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies, while rupture occurs in evaginating pore-free segments. NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution of NPCs, with pore-to-pore distance decreasing from ~200 nm to ~100 nm in pore-dense regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C52, C56, C57, C63, and C64 are strongly supported by EM data showing segregation of pore-free and pore-dense segments (Figure 6A), quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C), and observation of rupture in pore-free regions (Figure 7A). The conclusion that NPC-free membranes are generated by redistribution is a reasonable inference from the quantitative data showing increased NPC density in some regions and decreased density in others.

results.result: Nucleoplasmic bodies are dense, round structures (200-500 nm in diameter) that form by invagination of NPC-rich clusters. They often appear in a beads-on-a-string arrangement and are bounded by closely juxtaposed NPCs with intact central ring structures. As NPCs accumulate between pore-free spikes, the membranes in these NPC-rich dimples buckle into the nucleoplasm and invaginate to form nucleoplasmic bodies.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, C55, C58, C59, and C72 are well-supported by EM data showing nucleoplasmic bodies with precise measurements (Figures 5D, 6B), tomograms confirming NPC structure (Figures 6D, E), and examination of intermediates suggesting the invagination mechanism (Figures 6A, B). The proposed mechanism of formation is a reasonable inference from the structural intermediates observed.

results.result: The F-actin shell first appears as an equatorial band of foci when the NE is still intact and impermeable to large dextrans. Approximately 30-45 s later, as F-actin foci grow and merge to form a continuous shell, the first breaks appear allowing large dextrans to enter. During this process, spike-like membrane protrusions appear 10-15 s after F-actin foci begin to assemble, and NPCs appear to separate partially from the membrane. Dextran entry occurs 20-30 s after the initial membrane spikes, when membrane reorganization has progressed to an advanced stage.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C23 are directly supported by high-resolution live-cell imaging data (Figures 1A-D) showing the temporal sequence of events with precise timing. The observations are consistent across multiple experiments and provide a detailed timeline of the membrane reorganization process.

results.result: Membrane reorganization during NEBD is dependent on actin assembly. Inhibiting F-actin shell formation by depleting actin monomers or inhibiting Arp2/3 prevents membrane reorganization and the separation of lamina and membranes, though the nucleus still collapses and the NE ruffles due to partial NE disassembly. Without F-actin assembly, large membrane fragments remain intact long after NEBD.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C36 are supported by experimental data using UtrCH-mediated actin depletion (Figure 1E) and CK-666 inhibitor (Figure 3C), which demonstrate that preventing F-actin shell formation blocks membrane reorganization while allowing nuclear collapse. This provides strong functional evidence for the role of actin assembly in membrane reorganization.

results.result: The lamina co-localizes with F-actin at the base of the shell, while NPCs form a separate layer up to 500 nm above the F-actin shell. Before NE rupture, NPC and lamina stainings overlap at ~50 nm resolution, but at the shell stage, NPC-stained NE fragments 'float' above the intact lamina. The still-intact lamina serves as the scaffold upon which the F-actin shell assembles, while nuclear membranes fragment and separate away from the lamina and F-actin shell.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C35 are supported by immunofluorescence data with line profile analysis (Figures 3A, B), STED data showing separation of NPCs from lamina (Figure 3C), and comparison to pre-NEBD state (Figure 3C). The conclusion that lamina serves as a scaffold is a reasonable inference from the co-localization data.

results.result: The NE is smooth, continuous, and tightly packed with NPCs at regular spacing (~200 nm) in immature oocytes and intact regions. In areas closer to the rupture site, gaps in NPC occupancy appear and increase in number and size, evolving into bumps and membrane spikes that rise ~1 μm above the level of the NE.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C44 are directly supported by EM data (Figures 5A-D) with quantification (Figure 6C) and measurements from tomographic data (Figures 5D, E). The observations are consistent with previous work (Lénárt et al., 2003) and provide a detailed spatial progression of NE changes leading to rupture.

results.result: Membranes are interrupted in areas where segregation of pore-dense and pore-free regions is strongest and NPC invaginations are most dramatic. In these rupture areas, no continuous membrane boundary separates cyto- and nucleoplasm, but nucleoplasmic bodies are abundant. Light microscopy reveals a complex tubular-vesicular network densely labeled by NPC staining.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 are supported by EM montages showing rupture sites (Figure 7A) and STED microscopy showing tubular-vesicular networks (Figure 7B). The correlation between EM and light microscopy data strengthens the conclusion about the nature of membrane rupture.

results.result: The stage when 25-kDa dextran fills the nucleus but 160-kDa dextran is excluded identifies the time-window of F-actin shell formation and NE rupture. NE rupture initiates near the equator of the nucleus and spreads as a wave towards the poles.
results.evaluation: Claims C91 and C92 are supported by correlative light and EM data (Figures 4A-D) and are consistent with established knowledge about NE permeability during NEBD (Lénárt et al., 2003). The spatial arrangement of rupture is directly observed in EM montages and confirmed by live and fixed light microscopy.

results.result: NPC-free areas pushed out by the F-actin shell may cause crowding of NPCs in juxtaposed regions. Pore-free nuclear membranes separated from the lamina are unstable and rupture, rearranging into an ER-like reticular structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C48 and C73 are inferred from EM observations and quantification of NPC spacing (Figure 6C) showing increased density in some regions. While the authors acknowledge they cannot estimate 3D membrane areas from 2D sections, the inference is reasonable based on the observed redistribution of NPCs and rupture occurring in pore-free regions (Figure 7A).

results.result: F-actin foci form within the lamina when cytoplasmic components reach critical concentration due to NPC disassembly. Once triggered, foci grow rapidly due to autocatalytic Arp2/3-mediated nucleation. The asymmetry in filament growth may be explained by force-promoted nucleation of branched meshwork. The morphology is similar to in vitro F-actin networks on micropatterned Arp2/3, suggesting localized Arp2/3 activation within the lamina may be sufficient to explain the F-actin shell morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C66, C68, C69, and C70 are largely speculative or based on analogy to in vitro systems (Reymann et al., 2010; Bieling et al., 2016). While C66 is consistent with observed rapid growth (Figure 1A) and C70 is supported by Arp2/3 localization data (Figure 3E), the specific trigger mechanism (C65) and force-based explanation for asymmetry (C68) remain hypothetical. Additional experiments would be needed to directly test these mechanisms.

results.result: Detaching nuclear membranes from the lamin network leads to NE rupture in various physiological contexts including cancer cells, micronuclei, and migrating cells. In somatic cells, NEBD proceeds by microtubule-mediated tearing of the lamina, but a similar mechanism based on segregation of lamina, NPCs, and membranes may play a critical role in destabilizing the NE. The segregation of nuclear membranes from the lamin network appears to be a general feature of nuclear rupture in dividing mammalian somatic cells and during interphase NE rupture in cancer cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C78 and C90 are supported by citations to other work (Hatch et al., 2013; Thiam et al., 2016; Davidson and Lammerding, 2014; Denais et al., 2016; Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002), but the extension of the starfish oocyte mechanism to mammalian somatic cells (C78, C90) is speculative. The authors acknowledge that the precise morphology of NE intermediates in somatic cells at comparable resolution is not known, making this inference uncertain.

results.result: F-actin assembly may facilitate NE rupture by increasing membrane tension in evaginations or causing extreme membrane curvatures at invagination boundaries. The ESCRT machinery may be involved in membrane rearrangements during NEBD based on similarities in membrane topology to NE repair processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C79 and C80 are explicitly speculative. While the authors observe membrane topologies similar to those in ESCRT-mediated processes (Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016; Olmos et al., 2015), no direct evidence for ESCRT involvement or specific mechanisms of membrane rupture is provided. These remain hypotheses requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: F-actin shells similar to those in starfish oocytes have been observed in several species including sea urchin, Nematostella vectensis, and polychaete worms. F-actin-mediated NE rupture may be widely spread across animal species, and this mechanism is likely to function in many animal species.
results.evaluation: Claims C81, C82, and C89 are supported by citations showing F-actin shells in multiple species (Burkel et al., 2007; DuBuc et al., 2014; Jacobsohn, 1999). While the detailed characterization is lacking in these other species, the observation of similar structures across diverse taxa provides reasonable support for the inference that this mechanism may be widespread.

results.result: The clearing of NPCs off the membrane during NEBD appears to be conserved in organisms with partially open mitosis. In Ustilago maydis, microtubules tear the NE by pulling the nucleus through a small opening, and NPCs initiate release of nucleoporins prior to rupture. In Schizosaccharomyces japonicus, the NE is split by stretching the nucleus between poles, and NPCs are redistributed to the poles, freeing naked membranes at regions destined to be broken.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by citations to work in U. maydis and Sz. japonicus (Straube et al., 2005; Aoki et al., 2011; Theisen et al., 2008). The observation that NPC clearing occurs before NE rupture in these organisms, despite different rupture mechanisms, supports the authors' conclusion that this may be a conserved feature.

results.result: Background information on nuclear envelope structure, oocyte nuclear architecture, and established mechanisms of NEBD across species. The NE is composed of inner and outer membranes fused at NPCs, supported by the lamina. Oocytes have large nuclei densely packed with NPCs. NEBD begins with phosphorylation-driven partial permeabilization allowing small molecules to leak while maintaining overall NE structure. In mammalian cells, microtubules tear the NE in a dynein-dependent process.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C14 represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations (Burke and Ellenberg, 2002; Goldberg and Allen, 1995; Hetzer, 2010; Ungricht and Kutay, 2017; Dultz et al., 2008; Mühlhäusser and Kutay, 2007; Terasaki et al., 2001; Lénárt et al., 2003; Martino et al., 2017; Linder et al., 2017; Beaudouin et al., 2002; Salina et al., 2002). These provide necessary context for the current work.
